parsed.n_justification: The Naches River basin in central Washington requires multiple columns to capture the topographic gradient from Cascade Mountain hillslopes (~1500-2000m elevation) through mid-elevation forests (~800-1200m) to the valley floor (~300-500m). 15 columns arranged in 3 transects (upper, middle, lower basin) with 5 positions each (ridge, upper slope, mid slope, lower slope, valley) provide spatial coverage for characterizing vertical water table dynamics across the elevation and landscape gradient. However, these columns operate independently - true lateral flow and regional water table mapping would require PFLOTRAN in fully-coupled 3D mode or a distributed hydrologic model, which exceeds single-column ELM capabilities.
assumptions: Single-column ELM simulations provide only vertical water table dynamics at each location independently
No lateral groundwater flow or hydraulic connectivity between columns in standard ELM
Water table depth (ZWT) represents local perched or unconfined aquifer conditions only
Topographic position and soil texture serve as proxies for landscape position but do not enable flow routing
QCHARGE represents local recharge but not regional aquifer contribution
Spatial interpolation between column water tables would be purely statistical, not physically-based
True hillslope-to-valley flow requires PFLOTRAN 3D subsurface flow model or coupled surface-subsurface model
Inter-column exchange fluxes cannot be quantified without explicit lateral flow physics
Regional water table mapping would require post-processing interpolation with no physical flow constraints
Cascade Mountain snowmelt timing and rain-on-snow events are critical for recharge patterns
Bedrock depth and permeability structure unknown - assumed from regional geology
Valley aquifer may be confined/semi-confined - not represented in standard ELM soil column
Agricultural water use in lower valley not explicitly modeled without irrigation module
Results represent potential recharge zones and local water table response, not integrated groundwater system
